What Is a Reversible Reaction?

Most chemical reactions you have studied so far go in one direction — reactants turn into products and the reaction stops. But some reactions can go in both directions. In a reversible reaction, the products can react to reform the original reactants. We show this using the equilibrium symbol ⇌ instead of a normal arrow.

A classic example is the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride. When heated, ammonium chloride (a white solid) breaks down into ammonia and hydrogen chloride — two colourless gases. When these gases cool and meet, they recombine to form ammonium chloride again:

\(\text{ammonium chloride} \rightleftharpoons ammonia + \text{hydrogen chloride}\)
NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g)

You can see this in action: when you heat ammonium chloride in a test tube, a white solid forms higher up in the tube where the gases have cooled and recombined. This proves the reaction is reversible.

Key Fact

The ⇌ symbol tells you a reaction is reversible. A normal arrow (→) means the reaction only goes one way. Never use a normal arrow for a reversible reaction in the exam.

Hydrated Copper Sulfate — Another Reversible Reaction

Another important example is the hydration of copper sulfate. Hydrated copper sulfate is a blue crystalline solid. When you heat it, it loses its water of crystallisation and turns into a white powder called anhydrous copper sulfate:

\(\text{hydrated copper sulfate} (blue) \rightleftharpoons \text{anhydrous copper sulfate} (white) + water\)
CuSO4·5H2O(s) ⇌ CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l)

If you add water back to the white anhydrous powder, it turns blue again and gets hot — the reverse reaction is exothermic. This colour change is so reliable that anhydrous copper sulfate is used as a chemical test for the presence of water.

To test for the presence of water, add the liquid to white anhydrous copper sulfate. If the powder turns blue, water is present. This does not tell you the water is pure — to confirm pure water, check the boiling point (100 °C at standard pressure). Cobalt chloride paper can also be used: it turns from blue to pink when water is present.

Energy Changes in Reversible Reactions

In any reversible reaction, if the forward reaction is exothermic (gives out energy), then the reverse reaction is endothermic (takes in energy) — and vice versa. The amount of energy transferred in each direction is exactly the same.

For the copper sulfate example: the forward reaction (heating blue copper sulfate to drive off water) is endothermic — you have to supply heat energy. The reverse reaction (adding water to the white powder) is exothermic — the mixture gets hot. The energy released going one way equals the energy absorbed going the other way.

Key Fact

If a reversible reaction is exothermic in the forward direction, it is endothermic in the reverse direction — and the energy change is the same in both directions. This is a common exam question.

Dynamic Equilibrium

When a reversible reaction takes place in a closed system (where nothing can get in or out), something interesting happens. At first the forward reaction is fast because there are lots of reactants. As products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up. Eventually, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. This is called dynamic equilibrium.

“Dynamic” means that both reactions are still happening — molecules are constantly reacting in both directions. “Equilibrium” means the overall concentrations of reactants and products stay the same because the two rates are balanced. It is not a static situation where everything has stopped.

Key Fact

Dynamic equilibrium requires a closed system. The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so concentrations of reactants and products do not change — but the reaction has not stopped.

Le Châtelier’s Principle

Le Châtelier’s principle states that if a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in conditions, the position of equilibrium shifts to partially oppose that change. In other words, the system tries to “undo” whatever you did to it. This principle lets you predict which way the equilibrium will shift when you change temperature, pressure, or concentration.

If you increase the temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the endothermic direction to absorb the extra heat. If you decrease the temperature, the equilibrium shifts in the exothermic direction to release heat and restore the temperature. Changing temperature changes both the rate and the position of equilibrium — and therefore changes the yield of products.

Example: In a reversible reaction where the forward reaction is exothermic, increasing the temperature will favour the reverse (endothermic) reaction, producing more reactants and fewer products. The yield of products decreases.

For reactions involving gases, changing the pressure affects the equilibrium position. If you increase the pressure, the equilibrium shifts towards the side with fewer moles of gas — this reduces the pressure. If you decrease the pressure, the equilibrium shifts towards the side with more moles of gas.

Example: Consider N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g). The left side has 4 moles of gas (1 + 3) and the right side has 2. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right, producing more ammonia.

If you increase the concentration of a reactant, the equilibrium shifts to the right (forward direction) to use up the extra reactant, producing more products. If you increase the concentration of a product, the equilibrium shifts to the left (reverse direction) to use up the extra product.

Example: In the reaction A + B ⇌ C + D, adding more of substance A shifts the equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield of C and D until a new equilibrium is established.

Catalysts and Equilibrium

A catalyst speeds up both the forward and reverse reactions equally. This means a catalyst helps the system reach equilibrium faster, but it does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield of products. The same amounts of reactants and products are present at equilibrium whether a catalyst is used or not — you just get there more quickly.

Applying Equilibrium: The Haber Process

The Haber process is a real-world application of equilibrium principles. Nitrogen from the air reacts with hydrogen (from natural gas) to produce ammonia:

\(N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_{3}(g)\) — the forward reaction is exothermic.

Using Le Châtelier’s principle: a low temperature and high pressure would give the best yield of ammonia. However, low temperatures make the reaction too slow, so a compromise temperature of about 450 °C is used. High pressure (around 200 atmospheres) favours ammonia production. An iron catalyst is used to speed up the reaction without changing the yield. Any unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor.

Key Fact

The Haber process uses a compromise temperature (about 450 °C), high pressure (200 atm), and an iron catalyst. High pressure increases yield; the moderate temperature balances acceptable yield with a reasonable rate of reaction.

lessons.title: Materials, Corrosion, Haber Process and Fertilisers

before.content_html:
Corrosion

Corrosion is the destruction of a metal caused by reactions with substances in the environment. Most metals corrode when exposed to air and water over time. The most familiar example is the rusting of iron and steel.

Rusting is the corrosion of iron. It only happens when iron is in contact with both oxygen and water. The chemical name for rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Unlike the oxide layers on aluminium, rust is soft and flaky, so it falls away from the surface and exposes fresh metal underneath. This means rusting continues until all the iron has corroded.

Key Fact

Iron requires both oxygen and water to rust. Remove either one and rusting does not occur. This is the basis for all rust prevention methods.

Preventing Corrosion

Since rusting needs oxygen and water, prevention methods work by creating a barrier between the iron and these reactants, or by using a more reactive metal to protect the iron.

Painting: A layer of paint stops oxygen and water reaching the iron surface. Used on bridges, cars, and railings. If the paint is scratched or chips off, the iron underneath will rust.

Oiling or greasing: A thin coat of oil or grease creates a waterproof barrier. Used on moving parts such as bicycle chains and machine components, where paint would crack or wear off.

Electroplating: Coating the iron with a thin layer of another metal (such as tin, chromium, or nickel) using electrolysis. Tin cans are steel coated with tin. If the coating is breached, the iron underneath can still rust.

Galvanising: Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc. Zinc acts as a barrier, but it also provides sacrificial protection — even if the coating is scratched, the zinc corrodes instead of the iron because zinc is more reactive.

Sacrificial protection uses a block of a more reactive metal (usually zinc or magnesium) attached to or near the iron structure. The more reactive metal oxidises preferentially, donating electrons to the iron and preventing it from reacting. This method is used on ships’ hulls, underground pipes, and offshore oil rigs. The sacrificial block must be replaced periodically as it is gradually consumed.

Alloys

An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually other metals, but sometimes non-metals like carbon). Alloys are made because pure metals are often too soft for practical use. In a pure metal, the atoms are arranged in regular layers that can slide over each other easily. In an alloy, atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, making it harder for them to slide. This makes alloys harder and stronger than pure metals.

Key Fact

Most metals in everyday use are alloys, not pure metals. The different-sized atoms in an alloy disrupt the regular arrangement of layers, preventing them from sliding and making the alloy harder.

Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon (0.1–2% carbon). Low-carbon steel is easy to shape and used in car bodies. High-carbon steel is harder and used in cutting tools. Stainless steel contains chromium (and often nickel) and resists corrosion — used in cutlery, surgical instruments, and kitchen sinks.

Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin — hard and resistant to corrosion, used for statues and ship propellers. Brass is copper and zinc — harder than pure copper, used in musical instruments and plumbing fittings. Gold alloys are gold mixed with silver, copper, or zinc to make them harder — pure gold (24 carat) is too soft for jewellery.

Ceramics, Polymers, and Composites

Ceramics are non-metallic solids made by heating. Examples include clay pottery, bricks, and glass. Ceramics are very hard, resistant to heat and corrosion, but they are brittle — they shatter rather than bend when force is applied.

Composites are materials made by combining two or more different materials. Each component keeps its own properties, but together the composite has improved characteristics that neither material has alone. The two parts are a matrix (the background material that binds everything together) and a reinforcement (the material that adds strength or stiffness).

Concrete: Gravel or crushed stone (reinforcement) held together by cement (matrix). Strong in compression but weak in tension. Reinforced concrete: Steel bars or mesh (reinforcement) embedded in concrete (matrix) — strong in both compression and tension, used in buildings and bridges.

Fibreglass (GRP): Glass fibres (reinforcement) set in a polymer resin (matrix). Lightweight and strong, used in boat hulls, car body panels, and insulation. Carbon fibre reinforced polymer: Carbon fibres in a polymer resin. Extremely strong and lightweight, used in aircraft, racing cars, and tennis rackets.

The Haber Process

The Haber process is the industrial method for making ammonia (NH₃). Ammonia is a vital chemical because it is used to make fertilisers, nitric acid, and cleaning products. Without the Haber process, there would not be enough food to feed the world’s population.

The raw materials are nitrogen (obtained from the air by fractional distillation of liquid air) and hydrogen (obtained from natural gas or the cracking of hydrocarbons). The balanced equation is:

Key Fact

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

This reaction is reversible — it can go in both directions. The yield of ammonia is only about 15%, so unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled back through the reactor.

The conditions used in the Haber process represent a compromise between rate and yield:

Temperature: About 450 °C. The forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher yield. However, too low a temperature makes the reaction too slow. 450 °C is a compromise — fast enough to be economical, but the yield is only about 15%.

Pressure: About 200 atmospheres. There are 4 molecules of gas on the left (1 N₂ + 3 H₂) and only 2 on the right (2 NH₃). High pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer gas molecules — the products. Higher pressures would give even higher yields, but they are expensive and dangerous.

Catalyst: An iron catalyst is used. It speeds up the reaction so equilibrium is reached faster. The catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium or the yield — it just helps the system get there more quickly.

The forward reaction is exothermic, so Le Chatelier’s principle says a lower temperature would shift equilibrium to the right and increase yield. But at low temperatures, the particles have less kinetic energy, fewer successful collisions occur, and the rate of reaction is too slow to be practical. The chosen temperature (450 °C) gives a reasonable rate with an acceptable yield. The unreacted gases are recycled to maximise overall conversion.

Similarly, very high pressures would increase yield further, but the cost of building and maintaining equipment that can withstand extreme pressures, along with increased safety risks, means 200 atmospheres is the economically practical compromise.

NPK Fertilisers

NPK fertilisers contain three essential elements that plants need for healthy growth:

Nitrogen (N) — promotes leaf and stem growth. Phosphorus (P) — promotes root development and helps with energy transfer. Potassium (K) — helps with disease resistance, flower and fruit development, and overall plant health.

Without these minerals, crops grow poorly. Intensive farming removes these elements from the soil faster than natural processes can replace them, so farmers add fertilisers to maintain crop yields and feed growing populations.

Key Fact

The nitrogen in NPK fertilisers comes from ammonia (via the Haber process). Ammonia can be reacted with nitric acid to produce ammonium nitrate (NH₄NO₃), a widely used nitrogen fertiliser. Phosphorus comes from phosphate rock, and potassium comes from potassium chloride or potassium sulfate mined from the ground.

In the laboratory, NPK fertilisers can be made by mixing the correct proportions of compounds containing nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. For example, mixing ammonium sulfate (provides N), potassium phosphate (provides P and K), and potassium chloride (provides K) in the right ratio produces a balanced NPK fertiliser. Industrially, ammonium nitrate is produced by neutralising ammonia solution with nitric acid: NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃.
